title: Metropolitan Police announces exploration of AI to grade and triage child sexual abuse imagery to find unknown victims faster
summary: On 13 April 2026 the Met said it is exploring AI to grade and triage child sexual abuse imagery, testing with multiple companies, to flag unknown victims faster; no deployment or outcome yet.
account: The Metropolitan Police Service announced that it is exploring the use of artificial intelligence to support rapid grading and triage of child sexual abuse imagery. Material possibly relating to unknown victims could then be flagged for prioritized safeguarding. The force also wants to reduce officers' manual review of distressing material. It said it is in conversations with multiple companies and testing how this could work. It described a separate tool that reviews 641,000 messages in 35 minutes, and a £10 million investment in victim interview suites. It cited more than 5,400 child sexual abuse offenses investigated in the past year and over 1,300 children safeguarded. Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes said speed matters for safeguarding and that human judgment and oversight would remain central. The OECD AI Incidents Monitor records it as an “AI hazard”, noting the use is under consideration and not implemented.
purpose: Rapidly analyze seized imagery to grade it in categories A to C. Flag content possibly showing previously unknown victims. The aims are to prioritize safeguarding and reduce officer exposure.
system: Unnamed AI grading and triage tools under evaluation
domain: Child protection / online child sexual abuse investigation
taxonomy_note: Exploration only; the type names the triage bottleneck the Met wants to automate.

ratings.reason: No deployment or measured effect; the force describes intended benefits only.
No victim identified through the tools in the sources.

ai_role.statement: No AI system has yet acted. The Met is testing possible tools from unnamed companies. The case is included only as a documented official intention.
